findings.measured: Almost no content above 16 kHz; check whether an MP3/AAC or low-passed file was used as a source.

steps.text: Check the session for MP3 or AAC files, such as samples or imported references.
Look for a low-pass filter on the master or a bus cutting everything above 16 kHz.

findings.measured: Loudness range is 1.7 LU; there is little contrast between sections.

steps.text: Write volume automation (or use Clip Gain) so verses sit 2–3 dB below choruses.

other_options.text: Use Clip Gain on the verse clips so they sit 2–3 dB below the choruses.
Ease the mix-bus compressor: raise the threshold or slow the attack so transients get through.

notes.headline: This mix is technically clean and ready for mastering — the only things worth a look are a missing top octave above 16 kHz and a very flat 1.7 LU loudness range.
notes.summary: Nothing here is broken: at -17.11 LUFS integrated with -4.14 dBTP true peak, you've left plenty of headroom for mastering, and the stereo picture holds up in mono (0.91 dB mono loss, 0.969 low-end correlation). Two things are worth checking before you hand it off. There's almost no content above 16 kHz, which usually means a lossy source file or a low-pass somewhere in the chain, and the loudness range of 1.7 LU says the song sits at one level from start to finish.

priorities.title: Find out why there's nothing above 16 kHz
priorities.why: A hard cut at 16 kHz normally points to an MP3/AAC source or a low-pass left on a bus. Mastering can't put back air that was never printed, so it's worth tracing now rather than after the fact.

priorities.title: Add some section-to-section contrast
priorities.why: At 1.7 LU loudness range, verses and choruses are landing at the same level, so the arrangement won't lift where it should. This is a musical call, not a fault — but it's easier to shape in the mix than in mastering.

listen_for: Play the mix on headphones and listen to cymbals, hats and any air on vocals — do they sound dull or veiled in a way that fits the 16 kHz cut?
Go back through the session for imported samples or reference files and confirm none of them are MP3 or AAC.
After writing verse/chorus automation, play the first chorus entry and check it clearly lifts against the verse before it.
Check mono fold-down once more on a single speaker or phone — it should stay solid, which is what the 0.91 dB mono loss suggests.
strengths: -4.14 dBTP true peak and -17.11 LUFS give mastering all the headroom it needs.
Mono compatibility is strong: only 0.91 dB mono loss, and low-end correlation of 0.969 means the bass stays centered.
Left/right balance is within -0.39 dB, so nothing is pulling to one side.

judge.priority_order: F1 (permanent air loss, unfixable in mastering) is placed before F2 (fixable loudness range issue), correctly reflecting bigger audible consequence among equal info-severity findings.
judge.explains_impact: F1 explains that mastering can't restore missing air, and F2 explains that verses/choruses won't lift as they should, both describing listening impact rather than just numbers.
judge.groups_causes: The two findings have unrelated causes (high-frequency content vs. dynamic range) and are correctly kept as separate priorities rather than merged.
judge.specific: Notes reference the exact measurements (-17.11 LUFS, -4.14 dBTP, 0.91 dB mono loss, 1.7 LU) and specific findings from this bounce, not generic advice.
judge.stage_appropriate: Notes correctly frame headroom as a strength for mastering rather than judging loudness against release standards, matching the mix stage.
judge.faithful: All claims (headroom, mono compatibility, LR balance, air cutoff, LRA) accurately reflect the report's measurements and findings without contradiction.
judge.concise: The notes are focused and avoid excessive repetition or hype, matching the small number of findings in a clean report.
